title: GitLab mechanics
description: Writes references/forge.md into each forge skill for a project on GitLab, on GitLab.com or a Self-Managed or Dedicated instance: the GitLab MCP server's tools first, glab and glab api where they fall short or a step runs unattended, the tier each feature needs and how to check it, and dated GitLab sources. GitLab's MCP server is declared by gitlab-mcp.

content: # GitLab

Which contributor files GitLab recognises, where it looks for them, how vulnerability reports reach a maintainer, and what a group can share with its projects. GitLab calls a repository a project and a pull request a merge request. Every claim here was checked on 2026-10-20; sources are at the end.
## Contents
- Host, access and versions
- Tier
- What GitLab surfaces
- Vulnerability reporting
- Checking what the project has
- Templates and shared defaults
- Sources
## Host, access and versions

- **Host.** `git remote get-url origin` names it: `gitlab.com`, or a GitLab Self-Managed or Dedicated instance. `glab api` uses the authenticated host of the current Git directory, and `--hostname <host>` overrides it.

- **MCP first.** The project declares GitLab's MCP server as `gitlab`. `get_project` returns the visibility; `list_repository_tree` (with `path`, `ref`, `recursive`) shows which files exist at the root and under `.gitlab/`; `get_repository_file` (`project_id`, `file_path`, `ref`) reads an existing `CONTRIBUTING.md` or template as committed. No MCP tool reads the issue or Service Desk settings, so those go through glab.
- **Unattended runs**, with no person present to complete OAuth, use glab with the token `glab auth login` stored.
- **glab versions.** The commands here behave the same in 1.99.0 and 1.123.0. `glab api` has no `--jq` flag in either, so pipe to `jq`.
## Tier
Recognised files, confidential issues, Service Desk and project description templates are all in GitLab Free. Sharing templates across projects is not:
| Feature | Tier | Offering |
| Templates in `.gitlab/issue_templates/` and `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/`, including `Default.md` | Free | All |
| Default description set in project settings | Premium, Ultimate | All |
| Group-level description templates | Premium, Ultimate | All |
| Group file templates | Premium, Ultimate | All |
| Instance template repository | Premium, Ultimate | Self-Managed, Dedicated |
| Service Desk | Free | GitLab.com, Self-Managed |

To see the plan: on GitLab.com, `glab api namespaces/<top-level-group> | jq '{plan, trial}'`. On Self-Managed or Dedicated the plan comes from the instance licence, and `glab api license | jq .plan` needs an administrator; otherwise ask one. Where neither answers, `licensedFeatures { hasEpicsFeature }` on the namespace (GraphQL, an Experiment field) is true on Premium and above. Do not propose a Premium feature to a Free namespace without saying it needs an upgrade.
## What GitLab surfaces
The project overview links four files, and only when they are **at the repository root** on the default branch:
| File | Matched names | Surfaced as |
| README | `README`, `index` or `_index`, plain or with a markup extension | Rendered on the overview |
| Licence | `LICENSE`, `LICENCE`, `COPYING`, `UNLICENSE`, any extension | A link named after the detected licence |
| Changelog | Names starting `CHANGELOG`, `HISTORY`, `CHANGES` or `NEWS` | A link |
| Contributing | Names starting `CONTRIBUTING` | A link to the contributing guidelines |
Matching is case-insensitive. A `CONTRIBUTING.md` under `docs/` or `.gitlab/` is not found; put it at the root.

**`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `SUPPORT.md`, `CITATION.cff` and `GOVERNANCE.md` get no special handling.** They render as ordinary Markdown when opened, and nothing in the GitLab interface links to them. Keep the conventional filenames anyway, because readers and tools look for them, and link each one from the README or `CONTRIBUTING.md`, since nothing else will. GitLab has no sponsor button and no `FUNDING.yml`.
## Vulnerability reporting

GitLab has no private vulnerability reporting form for outside reporters. The vulnerability report (Ultimate) tracks scanner findings and is not a channel for them. The private channels are these, and `SECURITY.md` names whichever the project has:

- **A confidential issue** (Free). The reporter opens an issue and selects **Turn on confidentiality**. Only the author, assignees, and members with the Planner role or higher can see it, and it is hidden from search for everyone else. GitLab documents that a Guest can create one and see their own; it does not spell out a non-member on a public project, so give a direct contact as well.

- **Service Desk** (Free; GitLab.com and Self-Managed). The reporter emails the project's Service Desk address, needs no GitLab account, and GitLab creates a ticket that on a public project is always confidential.

For a public project, the strongest arrangement is a short `SECURITY.md` that says to open a confidential issue, links the new-issue page, and gives the Service Desk address or a direct contact. Never route vulnerabilities to a public issue or merge request.
## Checking what the project has
```bash
glab api projects/:id | jq '{visibility, issues_access_level, service_desk_enabled, service_desk_address}'

Issues must be enabled for a confidential-issue instruction to work, and Service Desk must be enabled before its address is published. Visibility is `public`, `internal` (every signed-in user of the instance) or `private`; treat internal as private for outside contributors. Do not describe a channel the project does not have.
## Templates and shared defaults

**GitLab has no equivalent of an account-wide repository of community files.** No group or instance setting supplies `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `SECURITY.md` or `SUPPORT.md` to projects that lack them, so each project carries its own. Group file templates (Premium) only offer a file as a starting point when someone creates one; they default nothing. **A licence cannot be defaulted** either way.
What can be shared is issue and merge request description templates:

- **Per project** (Free): Markdown files in `.gitlab/issue_templates/` and `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/`, on the default branch. One named `Default.md`, any case, pre-fills every new issue or merge request. Templates may carry quick actions, which run only if the submitter has permission for them.
- **Per group** (Premium, Ultimate): a project that is a direct child of the group holds the templates, and every project in the group can use them. Setting it needs the Owner role on the group.
- **Per instance** (Premium, Ultimate; Self-Managed and Dedicated): an administrator picks an instance template repository.

Precedence for the default issue description, highest first: the template set in project settings, then the parent group's `Default.md`, then the project's own `Default.md`. **So a group default beats the project's own file.** Merge requests add inheritance rules of their own, from commit messages and branch names.

For a maintainer with many projects in one group on Premium, a group template project gives one set of issue and merge request templates instead of many. The community files still have to be copied into each project.

# GitLab

What GitLab does with project metadata, and how to read and change it. GitLab calls a repository a project. Its findability metadata is the project description, the topics and the project avatar, all under **Settings > General > Naming, description, topics** and **Project avatar**. Every claim here was checked on 2026-10-20; sources are at the end.
## Contents
- Host, access and versions
- Tier
- Search
- Reading the current metadata
- Verifying topics
- Description
- Topics
- Homepage
- Project avatar, the preview image
- Stars
- Applying changes

## Host, access and versions

- **Host.** `git remote get-url origin` names it: `gitlab.com`, or a GitLab Self-Managed or Dedicated instance. Each instance has its own topics, its own Explore pages and its own audience, so research on gitlab.com says nothing about a self-managed instance. `glab api` uses the authenticated host of the current Git directory, and `--hostname <host>` overrides it. Other glab commands read `GITLAB_HOST`.

- **MCP first.** The project declares GitLab's MCP server as `gitlab`. `get_project` (`project_id` or `url`) returns visibility, default branch and web URL, but not the description, topics or avatar. `list_projects` with `search` and `search` with scope `projects` find comparable projects. No MCP tool reads topics or changes project settings, so those go through glab.
- **Unattended runs**, with no person present to complete OAuth, use glab with the token `glab auth login` stored.

- **glab versions.** Checked against 1.99.0 and 1.123.0. `glab api` has no `--jq` flag in either, so pipe to `jq`. `glab repo view --jq` and `glab repo search --jq` exist only in 1.123.0. There is no `glab repo edit`; the equivalent is `glab repo update`, with the same flags in both versions. `glab api` refuses unauthenticated requests in 1.99.0, even for public endpoints; 1.123.0 sends them.
## Tier

Everything this skill touches is in GitLab Free: project topics, description, avatar, Explore and basic search. Advanced search (Premium, Ultimate) and exact code search (Premium, Ultimate; GitLab.com and Self-Managed) add code search across projects, which is the only way README text becomes searchable across an instance.

To see the plan: on GitLab.com, `glab api namespaces/<top-level-group> | jq '{plan, trial}'`. On Self-Managed or Dedicated the plan comes from the instance licence, and `glab api license | jq .plan` needs an administrator; otherwise ask one. Where neither answers, `licensedFeatures { hasEpicsFeature }` on the namespace (GraphQL, an Experiment field) is true on Premium and above.
## Search

The Projects API `search` parameter and the `search` parameter of the MCP `list_projects` tool both match a project's **name, path and description**. Neither reads topics or the README. GitLab does not document field by field what the projects scope of the search page matches.

Topics are browsed instead: **Explore > Topics** lists every topic on the instance, and each topic page, `https://<host>/explore/projects/topics/<topic-name>`, lists its projects, filterable by language and sortable by date, name or number of stars. A topic also has an RSS feed of new projects.
README text is searchable only through code search: inside one project on every tier, across projects only with advanced or exact code search.
## Reading the current metadata
Visibility from MCP `get_project`, or everything at once:
```bash
glab api "projects/:id?license=true" | jq '{visibility, description, topics, license: .license.key, avatar_url, star_count}'

Visibility is `public`, `internal` or `private`. **Internal** projects are visible to every signed-in user of the instance and to nobody else. Treat an internal project as private for anything aimed outside the instance, but its description and topics still help colleagues searching the instance.

**Topic names are public even when the project is not.** Only people with access see which topics a project carries, but everyone, signed in or not, can see every topic that exists on the instance. Never put a client name, codename or anything sensitive in a topic.
## Verifying topics
```bash
curl -s "https://<host>/api/v4/topics?search=<candidate>" | jq '.[] | {name, total_projects_count}'
glab api "projects?topic=<candidate>&order_by=star_count&per_page=5" | jq '.[] | {path_with_namespace, description}'

The first lists matching topics with their project counts; it needs no token on gitlab.com, and `glab api "topics?search=<candidate>"` does the same with one. The second shows what a browser of that topic page finds.

Topics are free text shared across the instance. Matching is case-insensitive, names may contain spaces and capitals, and assigning a name that does not exist creates a new topic. gitlab.com, for example, has `postgresql` with about 3,850 projects beside `Go PostgreSQL` with three, and no `database-migrations` topic at all, while `migrations` has 39. **A near-duplicate spelling starts a new topic page with only this project on it**, so take the established spelling from the topic search rather than from GitHub habit.
## Description
Limited to 2,000 characters.
## Topics

GitLab documents no limit on the number of topics or their length. Its source code caps a topic name at 255 characters, ASCII only, with no line breaks. There is no lowercase-and-hyphens rule; follow the spelling the instance already uses.
GitLab detects a project's languages and Explore filters by them, so a language topic is usually redundant.
GitLab marks project topics as Beta.
## Homepage

**GitLab projects have no homepage or website field**, and the Projects API has none. Put the documentation, demo or product link on the README first screen instead. Leave a URL out of the description unless it is the project's only next step.
## Project avatar, the preview image

GitLab has no separate social preview. A shared project link shows the project avatar and the description: on gitlab.com the page's `og:image` is the avatar at 64 by 64 pixels with a small `summary` card. That is observed behaviour, not documented. So the avatar has to read at a very small size, and the name and category phrase belong in the description, not in the image.

The avatar is 200 KB or smaller, ideally 192 by 192 pixels, in BMP, GIF, ICO, JPEG, PNG or TIFF. With nothing uploaded, GitLab uses a file named `logo.png`, `logo.jpg` or `logo.gif` at the repository root; with neither, it shows the first letter of the project name. Setting it needs the Maintainer or Owner role, and it can be set through the API.
## Stars

Starring adds a project to the user's **Starred** projects list, and topic pages and the Projects API can sort by number of stars. GitLab documents no recommendation or ranking beyond that sort. Claim nothing more.
## Applying changes
All need the Maintainer or Owner role. Show the command and the exact value before running each, and run them one at a time.
| Change | Command |
| Description | `glab repo update --description "..."`, run in the repository. Flags in both versions: `--description` (`-d`), `--defaultBranch`, `--archive`. No topic or avatar flag |
| Topics | `glab api --method PUT projects/:id -f 'topics=postgresql,linter,cli'` |
| Avatar | `glab api --method PUT projects/:id --form "avatar=@logo.png"` |

**The topics call replaces the whole set.** There is no add or remove; send the complete list, current topics included. The API accepts a comma-separated string, which works with `-f` in both glab versions. 1.123.0 also documents `-F 'topics=["a","b"]'` as a JSON array; 1.99.0 does not document array parsing for `-F`, so use the comma form.

# GitLab

The forge is GitLab. An issue is a GitLab issue, one of GitLab's work item types, and a pull request is a GitLab **merge request**. Write "merge request" or "MR", never "pull request", in anything posted to GitLab.

- Relationships
- Work item types
- Labels
- Custom fields, status, weight, and health status
- Milestones and iterations
- Boards, roadmaps, and saved views

## Reaching the project
The host is gitlab.com or a self-managed or Dedicated instance. Read it from `git remote get-url origin`, never assume gitlab.com.

- **MCP first.** The project declares GitLab's MCP server as `gitlab` (`https://<host>/api/v4/mcp`, OAuth per person). Its work item tools take `project_id` or `group_id` as an ID or full path, or a `url`. A fine-grained personal access token also works; legacy, project, and group access tokens get `403`.

- **glab where MCP has no tool.** Inside the repository glab resolves the host from the Git remote. Elsewhere pass `-R` with the project's full URL, or `--hostname <host>` to `glab api`. `GITLAB_HOST` also sets the default host; glab 1.123.0 documents it in `glab auth login --help` and `glab config --help`, glab 1.99.0 documents neither.
- **Unattended runs**, such as a heartbeat agent with nobody to complete a browser login, use glab with the token `glab auth login` stored, not MCP.
## Check what the project has

Most of what separates GitLab's tiers is planning features, so check before relying on any of them. On GitLab.com the plan belongs to the **top-level group**; on Self-Managed and Dedicated it is the instance licence.
Ask the top-level group which licensed features it has:
```bash
glab api graphql -f query='query { namespace(fullPath: "<top-level-group>") { licensedFeatures {
hasEpicsFeature hasSubepicsFeature hasBlockedIssuesFeature hasLinkedItemsEpicsFeature
hasScopedLabelsFeature hasCustomFieldsFeature hasWorkItemStatusFeature hasIssueWeightsFeature
hasIterationsFeature hasIssuableHealthStatusFeature hasOkrsFeature hasQualityManagementFeature } } }'

`licensedFeatures` is marked Experiment in the GraphQL reference (introduced in 18.1, some fields in 18.3). On 2026-10-20 it answered for public groups on gitlab.com without authentication through glab 1.123.0; glab 1.99.0 refused the same query unauthenticated. The `plan` field (GraphQL, Experiment since 18.2; REST `GET /namespaces/:id`) returned `null` unauthenticated, since billing fields are restricted from 18.9; who may read it when signed in was not verified, so prefer `licensedFeatures`.

Then list the work item types this project can use. With MCP, `get_work_item_types` with `project_id` (or `group_id` for epics); it returns each type's name and enabled widgets, so it also shows which fields a type accepts.
On Self-Managed, also check the server: `get_mcp_server_version`, and remember that `save_work_item`, `get_work_item`, and `list_work_items` arrived in GitLab 19.4.
## Tiers at a glance
| Feature | Tier | Notes |
| Issues, tasks, incidents, confidential issues, linked items (relates to) | Free | |
| Milestones, labels, description templates in the repository, issue boards, saved views | Free | Saved views: GitLab.com and Self-Managed |
| Epics, issues as children of epics, blocking and blocked by | Premium | Epics are group-level |
| Scoped labels, iterations, weight, status, custom work item types | Premium | |
| Custom fields | Premium | GitLab.com and Self-Managed only |
| Default description in project settings, group-level templates, roadmaps | Premium | |
| Child epics (multi-level), linked epics, health status | Ultimate | |
| Objectives and key results, test cases, requirements | Ultimate | OKRs are behind a feature flag and not ready for production |
| Service Desk tickets | Free | GitLab.com and Self-Managed |
## Relationships
GitLab stores parent and child, and blocks and is blocked by, as data, the same principle as anywhere: never describe them in text.

- **Child items.** A task is a child of an issue (Free), and the two must be in the same project. An issue is a child of an epic (Premium), from any project, up to 5000 direct children per epic. Epics nest under epics to seven levels (Ultimate). An issue has at most one parent epic. Tasks have no children.

- **Linked items.** `relates to` is Free. `blocks` and `is blocked by` are **Premium**, and work across projects. Linking epics needs Ultimate. A blocked item shows a blocked icon in lists and boards, and closing it asks for confirmation. None of the documented work items list filters selects blocked work.
- On Free there is no blocking relationship. Write the blocker as a sentence with its link, and say why it blocks.
## Work item types

GitLab's types are Issue, Task, Incident (Free), Epic (Premium, groups only), Objective and Key result (Ultimate, behind a feature flag), Test case and Requirement (Ultimate), and Ticket (Service Desk). Premium and Ultimate groups can add custom types, up to 40 per top-level group including GitLab's own.

For a technical work order use **Issue**, and **Task** for a child that one merge request finishes. Use the native type rather than a title prefix. Do not create or enable types as a side effect of filing work.
## Labels

Project labels belong to one project; group labels apply to every project in the group. **Scoped labels** (`key::value`, Premium) are mutually exclusive within a key: adding `workflow::review` replaces `workflow::doing`. That makes them tempting for status and priority, which state, the linked merge request, and Linear already carry, so the house rules on labels apply unchanged.
Find labels with `search_labels` (`full_path`, `is_project`, optional `search` of up to ten terms), or `glab label list`.
## Custom fields, status, weight, and health status

- **Custom fields** (Premium; GitLab.com and Self-Managed): single-select, multi-select, number, and text, at most 50 active per top-level group and 10 per type. The house rule for custom fields applies: component, perhaps; never priority, effort, or dates.

- **Status** (Premium): To do, In progress, Done, Won't do, Duplicate, and custom lifecycles. Done and Canceled statuses close the item. Use it for state, which is the forge's to hold; do not use it as a progress system for Linear's plan.
- **Weight** (Premium) and **health status** (Ultimate, `onTrack`, `needsAttention`, `atRisk`) are estimation and progress signals. Linear owns both. Do not set them.
## Milestones and iterations

Milestones (Free) are project or group milestones with dates and progress. **Iterations** (Premium) are group-level time boxes in cadences, which is scheduling and belongs in Linear. Neither is used by default; the narrow milestone case is a release or version boundary.
## Boards, roadmaps, and saved views
Issue boards (Free; multiple group boards and configurable boards need Premium), roadmaps (Premium), and saved views (Free) all duplicate Linear's planning. Not used by default.
For a large migration whose tree is the plan, the tree view is the epic's **Child items** section (Premium), or an issue's child tasks on Free. No board or roadmap is needed.

Saved searches cover the rest: the work items list filtered to Open and label `agent-ready`, or `list_work_items` with `state: "opened"` and `label_name: ["agent-ready"]`. No documented filter selects blocked work; read the blocked icon or the item's linked items.
## Description templates

Templates are Markdown files in `.gitlab/issue_templates/` on the default branch (Free). There are no issue forms and no field validation. `Default.md` pre-fills every new issue; a default set in project settings, group-level templates, and instance templates need Premium. Templates may carry quick actions such as `/label`, executed only if the submitter has permission.

The house rule stands: no templates where the team and agents write every issue. Where there is no `.gitlab` directory, do not create one as a side effect. If a security template is ever wanted, the one worth having starts with `/confidential`.
## Closing patterns and closing reasons

A closing pattern in a merge request description or a commit message closes the issue when the merge request merges into, or the commit is pushed to, the **default branch**. The keywords are the Close, Fix, Resolve, and **Implement** families in any tense, so `Implements #12` closes `#12` too. One keyword followed by a list closes the whole list: `Closes #4, #6` closes both. Text such as `Part of #123`, `Refs #123`, or `Related to #123` matches no pattern and closes nothing.
Across projects use `group/project#123` or the full URL. Maintainers can turn off automatic closing per project, and Self-Managed administrators can change the pattern, so check before relying on it.

GitLab Free has one closed state and no closing reason. Close with one line saying what changed. With **status** (Premium), set **Won't do** for work no longer needed. Mark a duplicate with `/duplicate #123`, which closes it and links the original.
## References and permalinks
| Reference | Form |
| Issue or task, same project | `#123` |
| Issue, other project | `group/project#123`, or `project#123` in the same group |
| Any work item | `[work_item:123]`, `[work_item:group/project/123]` |
| Epic | `&123` or `group&123` |
| Merge request | `!123`, `group/project!123` |
| Label, milestone | `~"key::value"`, `%"v3.0"` |

A permalink that uses the full 40-character commit SHA and ends with a line anchor (`#L27-30`), pasted alone in its paragraph in a comment or a description, embeds as a highlighted snippet (GitLab 19.5 and later). It must point to the same instance; over 100 lines, past line 5000, or more than ten embeds in one document are not embedded, and readers who cannot see the other project get the plain link. A branch or tag link never embeds.
## Rendering

Diagrams render from `mermaid` fences, and from `plantuml` where PlantUML is on (on gitlab.com it is; on Self-Managed an administrator enables it). Kroki diagrams need an administrator to enable Kroki. There are no `geojson`, `topojson`, or `stl` fences; GitLab renders `.geojson` files in the repository, not in issues.

Alerts (`> [!note]`, `tip`, `important`, `caution`, `warning`) exist from GitLab 17.10; the house rule is at most one. Task lists also accept `[~]` for an inapplicable item. `<details>` collapses long evidence.
## Security reports

GitLab has **no private vulnerability reporting or repository security advisory**; no equivalent was found in its documentation on 2026-10-20. The private route is a **confidential issue** (Free): only project members with the Planner role or above, and assignees, can see it. A Guest can create one and see only their own. A confidential issue's child tasks must be confidential too.
- Create it confidential from the start: `save_work_item` with `confidential: true`, `glab issue create --confidential`, or `/confidential`.
- Write it as the private-repository case: behaviour and impact, no working recipe in the body.
- Reporters outside the project can use Service Desk where the project has it; its tickets are confidential by default (GitLab.com and Self-Managed).
- On gitlab.com a public project can request a CVE ID from the confidential issue.
- The vulnerability report (Ultimate) tracks scanner findings. It is not a reporting channel.

# GitLab
This project's forge is GitLab. A pull request here is a GitLab merge request (`!123`): call it a
merge request in everything you write. A thread is a discussion, a comment is a note, and a line
comment is a diff note. Every command here is for the agent. Posting, replying, resolving and
approving each need the approval the skill's mutation table sets.
## Reaching GitLab
Use the MCP server first: the project declares it as `gitlab`, at `https://<host>/api/v4/mcp`, and
each person signs in with OAuth when their client first connects (a fine-grained personal access
token also works; legacy, project and group tokens get `403`). Where a tool does not cover an
operation, use `glab`.
The host is the one `git remote get-url origin` names: gitlab.com, or a Self-Managed or Dedicated
instance. Inside the repository `glab` uses that host once `glab auth login` has been run for it;
elsewhere, pass `-R https://<host>/<group>/<project>`, or set `GITLAB_HOST`.
`save_merge_request_review` needs GitLab 19.4 or later, `save_note` 19.2 (its older name
`create_merge_request_note` still works), and `get_merge_request`'s `include` 19.3. On an older
Self-Managed instance, use `glab`.
**Neither `save_note` nor `save_merge_request_review` accepts a line starting with `/`**, because
GitLab would run it as a quick action. Reword such a line.
## Tiers
Comments, threads, resolving, suggestions and optional approvals are Free. Blocking a merge by
requesting changes, and required approval rules, are Premium. To check the tier, see whether
`glab api metadata` reports `"enterprise": false` (Community Edition, Free only), then read `plan`
from `glab api namespaces/<top-level-group>`, which may be returned only on gitlab.com or to group
owners. Failing that, `licensedFeatures { hasEpicsFeature }` on the namespace (GraphQL, an
Experiment field) is true on Premium and above. When none answers, say which behaviour depends on
the tier.
## Reading the review
- MCP: `get_merge_request` with `include: ["discussions"]`, or `include: ["notes"]`, whose notes each
carry their `position` (file and line) and their `discussion` (id and whether it is resolved). The
response also counts `resolvedDiscussionsCount` and `resolvableDiscussionsCount`. One facet per
call; page with `notes_first` and `notes_after`.
- glab: `glab mr note list <iid> --state unresolved -F json`, or `glab mr view <iid> --unresolved`.
The JSON keeps each discussion's full `id`; text output shows its first eight characters.
## Replying in a thread
- MCP: `save_merge_request_review` with `method: "reply_discussion"`, `discussion_id` (bare or
global) and `body`. `save_note` with `discussion_id` also replies, but takes only the global form,
`gid://gitlab/Discussion/<id>`.
- glab: `glab mr note create <iid> --reply <discussion id or its first 8+ characters> -m "<reply>"`.
- API: `glab api projects/:id/merge_requests/<iid>/discussions/<discussion id>/notes -f body='<reply>'`.
## Resolving a thread
- MCP: `save_merge_request_review` with `method: "resolve_discussion"`, `discussion_id` and
`resolved: true` (`false` reopens it).
- glab: with the merge request's branch checked out, `glab mr note resolve <discussion id>`, and
`glab mr note reopen <discussion id>` to undo. To name the merge request as well, use the API form.
- API: `glab api -X PUT "projects/:id/merge_requests/<iid>/discussions/<discussion id>?resolved=true"`.
The author and anyone with the Developer role or above can resolve. Where the project's merge checks
include **All threads must be resolved** (`only_allow_merge_if_all_discussions_are_resolved` in
`glab api projects/:id`), an open thread blocks the merge, so resolving one changes what can merge.
A project can also resolve diff threads automatically when a push makes their lines outdated.
## Leaving comments
- **A line comment**: `save_merge_request_review` with `method: "create_diff_note"`, `new_path` and
`new_line` (or `old_path` and `old_line` for a removed line), and `body`; or
`glab mr note create <iid> --file <path> --line <n> -m "<comment>"`, with `--line 10:15` for a range.
- **A review**: `save_merge_request_review` with `method: "submit_review"`, 1 to 20 `comments`
(each `file`, `body`, optional `new_line`, `old_line`, `suggestion`) and a `summary`, posted in one
call. glab 1.123.0 can collect pending comments with `glab mr note draft create` and post them with
`glab mr note draft publish`; 1.99.0 has no pending comments.
- **A top-level comment**: `save_note` or `save_merge_request_review` with `method: "create_note"`;
or `glab mr note create <iid> -m "<comment>"`.
- **A suggestion** is a block in a diff note. `-0+0` replaces the commented line; `-2+2` replaces
two lines above it to two below, up to 100 each way:
````markdown
```suggestion:-0+0
return retries * backoff
The author, or anyone with the Developer role or above, applies it from the merge request: GitLab
commits it, authored by the reviewer who suggested it, and resolves the thread.
`save_merge_request_review` also has `approve`, and `submit_review` a `verdict`, which is only text
put in front of the summary. Approving, and requesting changes from the merge request page, are
never an agent's to do.
## Deferred work
A deferred item becomes a GitLab issue, linked from the thread. On the merge request, **Create issue
to resolve thread** opens one from a thread and resolves it.

# GitLab
This project's forge is GitLab. The pull request is a GitLab merge request: call it a merge request
in the prompt, the note's sentence and the reply. Every command here is for the agent, run
unattended.
GitLab records every push as a push event in the project's activity, so a remote copy pushed before
the opening time would show the new dates early.
Nothing here depends on the tier: merge requests, drafts and `glab` work on Free, Premium and
Ultimate, on gitlab.com, Self-Managed and Dedicated alike.
## Signing in for an unattended run
The run at the opening time has nobody to sign in, so it opens the merge request with `glab` and the
token `glab auth login` stored, never through the MCP server, whose OAuth sign-in needs a person and
a browser.
**The token must be set up before scheduling**, by the user, on this machine, for this host. The host
is the one `git remote get-url origin` names, gitlab.com or a Self-Managed or Dedicated instance:
```sh
glab auth login --hostname <host>    # the user runs this; a personal access token with the api and write_repository scopes
glab auth status                     # the agent checks it, in the worktree, from its own shell
`glab auth status` must report the remote's host as signed in. Prefer a personal access token to an
OAuth sign-in (`--web`): glab refreshes an OAuth token on use and has to store the new one, which
fails where it cannot write to its credential store, and an expired session stops the run. A
`GITLAB_TOKEN` in the agent's environment overrides the stored token, so check that too.
glab 1.123.0 stores the token in the operating system's keyring by default (the macOS Keychain);
1.99.0 stores it in `~/.config/glab-cli/config.yml` unless `--use-keyring` is passed. Either way,
the check above, run where the agent runs, is what counts.

## Reaching the project

Use the project's `gitlab` MCP server first (OAuth per person; a fine-grained personal access token also works). ## Check what the project has
What the passes may expect depends on the plan, which on gitlab.com belongs to the top-level group and on Self-Managed or Dedicated to the instance licence:
```bash
glab api graphql -f query='query { namespace(fullPath: "<top-level-group>") { licensedFeatures {
hasBlockedIssuesFeature hasEpicsFeature hasSubepicsFeature hasScopedLabelsFeature
hasCustomFieldsFeature hasWorkItemStatusFeature hasIssueWeightsFeature hasIterationsFeature
hasIssuableHealthStatusFeature } } }'
The fields are marked Experiment in the GraphQL reference. Blocking, epics, scoped labels, custom fields, status, weight, and iterations are Premium; child epics and health status are Ultimate.
## Reading the set

- MCP `list_work_items` with `project_id` (or `group_id` for the whole group), `state: "opened"`, and the scope's filter: `label_name`, `milestone_title`, `types` (`["ISSUE", "TASK"]`), `updated_before` for long-quiet items, `first` up to 100 with `after` to page. Results are compact: ID, IID, title, state, URL, type, and timestamps.

- MCP `get_work_item` with `project_id` and `work_item_iid` for the full body, labels, milestone, and parent; add `include: ["discussions"]` for threads with their resolved state, `["notes"]` for a flat history, or `["related_merge_requests"]`, one facet per call.
- glab: `glab issue list` with `-l`, `--search`, `-m`, `-a`, `-P 100`, `-O json`; `glab issue view <iid> --comments`. Both glab 1.99.0 and 1.123.0 have these; `--jq` exists only in 1.123.0.
## Missed closure

- `get_work_item` with `include: ["related_merge_requests"]`, then check whether one merged. Or `list_merge_requests` with `project_id`, `state: "merged"`, and `search: "#<iid>"`; or `glab mr list --merged --search "#<iid>"`.

- A closing pattern closes an issue when its merge request merges into the default branch. The keywords are the Close, Fix, Resolve, and **Implement** families, and one keyword followed by a list closes every issue in it: `Fixes #4, #6` closes both. A partial merge request that used one closed the issue early; partial merge requests use `Part of #n`.

- A project can turn automatic closing off, and Self-Managed administrators can change the pattern. An open issue whose closing merge request merged may be that, not neglect; check before calling it missed.
## Closing reasons and duplicates
- Duplicates: `/duplicate #<original>` closes the item and links it to the original. That is the native mechanism; propose it rather than a comment.
- GitLab Free has a closed state and no closing reason, so abandoned work closes with a one-line comment saying why. Where status exists (Premium), propose **Won't do**, which closes the item.
## Platform limits that are not findings
- On Free there is no blocking relationship. A blocker written as a sentence with a link is correct.
- A task and its parent issue must be in the same project. Work in another project is a sibling issue with a link, or a child of an epic on Premium.
- Tasks have no children; issues have tasks as children and epics as parents.
- Blocking links can cross projects on Premium, so a cross-project dependency stored as a relationship is fine there.
- Alerts exist from GitLab 17.10; the house rule is at most one.
## Metadata the passes check
- **Labels**: list them with `search_labels` (`full_path`, `is_project`) or `glab label list`. Group labels apply across projects, so check a label's level before proposing to delete it.

- **Scoped labels** (`key::value`, Premium) such as `priority::high` or `workflow::doing` encode priority or status. Priority belongs to Linear; status belongs to the issue's state or, on Premium, its **Status**. Propose subtraction.
- **Custom fields** (Premium): a label duplicating one loses to the field; a field for priority, effort, or dates duplicates Linear.
- **Weight**, **health status**, **iterations**, start and due dates set on issues duplicate Linear's estimates, health, cycles, and dates.
- **Milestones** that track a product plan rather than a release or version boundary duplicate Linear.
- **Epics, boards, and roadmaps** used as a product plan duplicate Linear. The only sanctioned use is a temporary epic tree for a large migration.
## Description templates

Templates are Markdown in `.gitlab/issue_templates/`, with `Default.md` pre-filling every new issue; Premium projects can also set a default in project settings, and groups can share templates. There are no issue forms, so the form tests apply to template headings and any quick actions in them. The one template artefact worth adding is a security template that starts with `/confidential`, since GitLab has no private vulnerability reporting and a confidential issue is its private route.

# GitLab
This project's forge is GitLab. A pull request here is a GitLab merge request: call it a merge
request in everything you write, reference it as `!123` (an issue is `#123`), and say draft, not
work in progress. Every command here is for the agent; none of it belongs in a description.
## Reaching GitLab
**Use the MCP server first.** The project declares GitLab's MCP server as `gitlab`, at
`https://<host>/api/v4/mcp`. Each person signs in with OAuth when their client first connects; a
fine-grained personal access token also works, while legacy personal, project and group access
tokens get `403 Forbidden`. Where a tool below does not cover an operation, use `glab`, or
`glab api` for the REST API.
**The host** is whatever `origin` points at: gitlab.com, or a GitLab Self-Managed or Dedicated
instance.
```bash
git remote get-url origin        # git@gitlab.example.com:group/project.git → gitlab.example.com
Inside the repository `glab` takes the host from that remote once `glab auth login` has been run
for it. Elsewhere, set `GITLAB_HOST=<host>`, pass `-R https://<host>/<group>/<project>` to `glab mr`
commands, or `--hostname <host>` to `glab api`. In `glab api` paths, `:id` and `:fullpath` expand to
the current repository's project.
**Tool availability follows the instance's GitLab version.** `save_merge_request` has that name from
GitLab 19.3; from 18.5 to 19.2 it is `create_merge_request`, which takes a description and reviewers
only from 18.8. `get_merge_request` takes `include` from 19.3, `list_merge_requests` arrived in
19.3, `get_project` in 19.4. On an older Self-Managed instance, or where access to the MCP server
has not been allowed for the top-level group (gitlab.com) or the instance, use `glab`.
## Tiers
GitLab's features split by tier: Free, Premium and Ultimate. The tier belongs to the top-level group
on gitlab.com, and to the instance's licence on Self-Managed and Dedicated. Check it before relying
on a Premium feature:
```bash
glab api metadata                       # "enterprise": false means Community Edition: Free features only
glab api namespaces/<top-level-group>   # "plan": free, premium or ultimate
The docs say `plan` might be returned only on gitlab.com or to group owners, so its absence proves
nothing; on Self-Managed the licence itself (`glab api license`) needs administrator access. Then
let the work item features stand in for the plan, as the issue skills check them:
`glab api graphql -f query='query { namespace(fullPath: "<top-level-group>") { licensedFeatures { hasEpicsFeature hasIssuableHealthStatusFeature } } }'`
reports epics on Premium and above and health status on Ultimate (an Experiment field; it lists no
merge request feature). When none of these answers, say which feature depends on the tier rather
than assuming it.
| Feature | Tier |
| Draft merge requests, closing patterns, commit templates, squash options, templates in `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/` | Free |
| Default description set in project settings | Premium |
| Code owners, required approval rules, more than one reviewer, title validation | Premium |
| Automatic assignment of code owners as reviewers | Premium, from GitLab 19.1 |
| Changing the closing pattern itself | Self-Managed and Dedicated administrators only |
## Draft and ready
- A merge request is a draft when its title starts with `Draft:`, `[Draft]` or `(Draft)`. A draft
cannot merge until it is marked ready.
- **Open a draft** with `glab mr create --draft`, or with `save_merge_request` and the title prefixed
with `Draft: `. `save_merge_request` has no draft parameter; the title is the flag.
- **Mark it ready** with `glab mr update <iid> --ready`, or with `save_merge_request`, its
`merge_request_iid` and the title without the prefix. Back to draft: `glab mr update <iid> --draft`.
The `/ready` quick action works in a comment typed by a person, but `save_note` and
`save_merge_request_review` refuse lines that start with `/`.
- Pushing a commit whose message starts with `draft:`, `Draft:`, `fixup!` or `Fixup!` to the source
branch marks the merge request draft, and a later commit does not undo it.
- Marking ready notifies participants, and on Premium, with automatic reviewer assignment on, it
assigns code owners as reviewers. Marking ready is therefore also a review request.
## Linking issues
A closing pattern in the description or in a commit message closes the issue when the merge request
merges into the default branch, or when the commit is pushed to it. The default words are `Close`,
`Fix`, `Resolve` and `Implement` in their usual forms (`Closes`, `Fixed`, `Resolving`), followed by
`#4`, `group/project#4` or the issue's URL: `Closes #4, #6`.
- An administrator of a Self-Managed or Dedicated instance can change the pattern, so on those
instances check with the user before relying on a word outside the default list.
- A project can turn closing off (`autoclose_referenced_issues` is `false`, below); the references
stay, and nothing closes.
- `Related to #5` marks the issue as related without closing it, and `Part of #5` only mentions it.
- `glab mr issues <iid>` lists the issues a merge request will close.
## What the merge keeps
Read the project's merge settings:
```bash
glab api projects/:id | jq '{merge_method, squash_option, squash_commit_template, merge_commit_template, autoclose_referenced_issues, merge_request_title_regex}'
- `squash_option` is `never` (Do not allow), `default_off` (Allow), `default_on` (Encourage) or
`always` (Require). Each merge request also carries its own `squash`, which `glab mr view <iid> -F json`
shows.
- **A squash keeps only what the squash template writes**, and the default template is `%{title}`:
the merge request title and nothing else, so the commit bodies do not reach the target branch.
- `merge_method` `merge` and `rebase_merge` keep the commits and add a merge commit; `ff` keeps the
commits and adds nothing. The default merge commit message is:
```text
Merge branch '%{source_branch}' into '%{target_branch}'
%{title}
%{issues}
See merge request %{reference}
- A `null` template is the default one. A template can pull in `%{description}` or
`%{all_commits}`, in which case the description or every commit message is kept too.

## Titles
GitLab renders a code span in a merge request title, so backticks show as code on the merge request
page. Titles support only code spans, emoji, links and references such as `#123` and `!456`; bold,
italic and other markdown appear as typed.
On Premium a project can set a title pattern (`merge_request_title_regex`, with
`merge_request_title_regex_description` as its example). A title that does not match blocks the
merge, and from GitLab 19.5 the draft prefix is ignored when matching. A pattern that lists scopes
counts as a written-down list.
## Description templates
Templates are `.md` files in `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/` on the default branch. `Default.md`
(any case) pre-fills every new merge request. On Premium, a default description in the project's
merge request settings (`merge_requests_template` in the API) takes priority over `Default.md`.
Groups (Premium) and Self-Managed or Dedicated instances (Premium) can share templates with their
projects.
Read a template with `get_repository_file` (`project_id`, `file_path`, `ref: "HEAD"`), or from the
checkout. `glab mr create --template <name>` loads one from the local checkout only.
## Reviewers, code owners and approvals
- `CODEOWNERS` lives at the root, in `docs/` or in `.gitlab/`, checked in that order; the first one
found is used. Code owners are Premium.
- Code owners do not request themselves. With **Automatically assign all code owners as reviewers**
on (Premium, GitLab 19.1 and later), GitLab assigns them when a merge request opens ready or a
draft is marked ready, and skips a draft or one that already has a reviewer.
- Free has optional approvals from anyone with the Developer role or above. Required approval
rules, and code owner approval on protected branches, are Premium. `glab mr approvers <iid>` lists
who can approve, and `get_merge_request` with `include: ["approvals"]` shows the state.
- Request a reviewer with `save_merge_request` and `reviewers` (usernames), or
`glab mr update <iid> --reviewer +<username>`. A `reviewers` list replaces the current one. Free
allows one reviewer per merge request; more than one is Premium.
## Opening and editing
| Operation | MCP | glab |

| Open | `save_merge_request`: `project_id`, `title`, `source_branch`, `target_branch`, `description` | `glab mr create --source-branch <branch> --target-branch <base> --title "$(cat title)" --description "$(cat body.md)" --yes` |
| Edit title or description | `save_merge_request` with `merge_request_iid` | `glab mr update <iid> --title … --description …` |
| Find one for a branch | no branch filter in `list_merge_requests` | `glab mr list --source-branch <branch> --all` |
| Read it, its commits or its diff | `get_merge_request` with `include: ["commits"]` or `["diffs"]` (one facet per call) | `glab mr view <iid>`, `glab mr diff <iid>` |
The branch must already be on the remote; `glab mr create` pushes only with `--push` or `--fill`.
## Checks
GitLab's checks are the merge request's pipelines: `get_merge_request` with
`include: ["pipelines"]`, or `glab ci status --branch <branch>`. No pipeline means the project runs
no CI for the branch, which is not a failure.
## Renaming a branch
A merge request's source branch cannot be changed: the update API takes a new target branch, never a
new source. A renamed branch is a new branch, so it needs a new merge request, while the old one
stays on the old name and loses its source once that branch is deleted.

The host is gitlab.com or a self-managed or Dedicated instance; read it from `git remote get-url origin`.

- **MCP first.** The project declares GitLab's MCP server as `gitlab`. Its tools take `project_id` (ID or full path, such as `group/project`) or `url`. It authenticates each person with OAuth; a fine-grained personal access token also works, and legacy, project, and group tokens get `403`.

Blocking relationships, epics, weight, iterations, and health status depend on the plan, which on gitlab.com belongs to the top-level group and on Self-Managed or Dedicated to the instance licence. Before proposing any of them:
```bash
glab api graphql -f query='query { namespace(fullPath: "<top-level-group>") { licensedFeatures {
hasBlockedIssuesFeature hasEpicsFeature hasSubepicsFeature hasIssueWeightsFeature
hasIterationsFeature hasIssuableHealthStatusFeature hasScopedLabelsFeature } } }'

The fields are marked Experiment in the GraphQL reference. Then call `get_work_item_types` with `project_id` for the types this project can create; Task and Issue are there on every tier, Epic only for groups on Premium or Ultimate.
| Relationship | Tier |
| Task as a child of an issue, same project | Free |
| Linked item, `relates_to` | Free |
| Issue as a child of an epic | Premium |
| `blocks` and `blocked_by` | Premium |
| Epic as a child of an epic, up to seven levels | Ultimate |
On Free, a blocker is a sentence with a link, never a relationship.
## Search before creating
- MCP: `list_work_items` with `project_id`, `search` (title and description), and `state: "opened"`; or `search` with `scope: "work_items"`, `search`, and `project_id`.
- glab: `glab issue list --search "<terms>"`, which searches title and description by default.
## Creating and editing
MCP `save_work_item` creates when `work_item_iid` is omitted and updates when it is given. Send only the fields you mean to set.
| Parameter | Use |
| `project_id` | The project, as ID or full path |
| `title`, `type_name` | Required on create; `type_name` is `Issue` or `Task` here |
| `description` | The body, GitLab Flavored Markdown |
| `labels` | Label names, create only; on update `add_labels` and `remove_labels` |
| `milestone` | A milestone title, only for a release or version boundary |
| `confidential` | `true` for a security report, set at creation |
| `parent_id` | The parent's global ID, `gid://gitlab/WorkItem/<id>` |
| `state` | Update only: `closed` or `opened` |

`save_work_item` returns an error for a label or milestone it cannot find. It never creates one, which is what the house rule needs. Do not set `weight`, `health_status`, `start_date`, or `due_date`: Linear owns estimates and dates.
glab fallback, in both 1.99.0 and 1.123.0:
```bash
glab issue create -t "<title>" -d "<body>" --yes
glab issue create -t "<title>" -d "<body>" -l agent-ready --confidential --yes
glab issue update <iid> -d "<body>"
glab issue update <iid> -l <label> -u <label>

**`glab issue create -l` and `glab issue update -l` go through the REST API, which creates any label that does not exist.** Check first with `search_labels` (`full_path`, `is_project: true`, `search`) or `glab label list`, and drop a label that is not there rather than creating it.
`--description-file` (read the body from a file or standard input) exists only in glab 1.123.0; with 1.99.0 pass the body with `-d`.
## Child items
A task under an issue:
- MCP: `save_work_item` with `type_name: "Task"`, `title`, and `parent_id` set to the issue's global ID. The task must be in the issue's project.
- In a description or comment typed in GitLab: `/set_parent #<issue>` on the task, or `/add_child #<task>` on the issue.

An issue under an epic (Premium): `save_work_item` with `parent_id` set to the epic's global ID; or `glab issue create --epic <epic-id>`, which takes the epic's ID rather than its `&` number; or `/epic &<epic>` typed in GitLab.

Read a global ID from `list_work_items`, whose results carry both the ID and the IID, or from `glab api projects/:fullpath/issues/<iid>`, whose `id` field is the number in `gid://gitlab/WorkItem/<id>`. **It is not the `#` number**, which is the IID. `glab work-items create --type task` creates a task but has no parent flag in either glab version, so set the parent afterwards:
```bash
glab api graphql -f query='mutation { workItemUpdate(input: {
id: "gid://gitlab/WorkItem/<child-id>",
hierarchyWidget: { parentId: "gid://gitlab/WorkItem/<parent-id>" } }) { errors } }'
`glab work-items` is marked experimental in both versions.

Premium and Ultimate only. Express them from the blocked item:

## Platform constraints
All verified on 2026-10-20:
- **Dependencies can cross projects**, unlike on some forges, but need Premium. On Free none exist.

- **Tasks cannot cross projects**: a task and its parent issue must be in the same project. Separable work in another project is an issue, under an epic on Premium, or a sibling issue with a link on Free.
- **Tasks have no children.** An issue's children are tasks; an issue's parent is an epic.

- **Limits**: 5000 direct children per epic, seven levels of epics, one parent epic per issue, ten items per `link_work_items` call. All are far above the house conventions, so they should never bind.

## Host, access and versions

- **Host.** `git remote get-url origin` names it: `gitlab.com`, or a GitLab Self-Managed or Dedicated instance. `glab api` uses the authenticated host of the current Git directory, and `--hostname <host>` overrides it. A self-managed instance may run an older GitLab than the documentation describes: `glab api version | jq .version` says which.

- **MCP first.** The project declares GitLab's MCP server as `gitlab`. `get_project` returns visibility, default branch and web URL; `get_repository_file` (`project_id`, `file_path`, `ref`) reads the README as committed, which is the version visitors see; `list_repository_tree` checks that a relative link's target exists on the default branch; `get_user` (`username`) resolves a maintainer's `name` and `web_url`. The licence and owner come from glab.
- **Unattended runs**, with no person present to complete OAuth, use glab with the token `glab auth login` stored.
- **glab versions.** The commands here behave the same in 1.99.0 and 1.123.0. `glab api` has no `--jq` flag in either, so pipe to `jq`; `glab repo view --jq` exists only in 1.123.0.
## Tier

Nothing here depends on the tier: README rendering, GitLab Flavored Markdown, stars, following and notifications are all in GitLab Free. Two diagram types depend on the instance instead: PlantUML is enabled on gitlab.com and needs an administrator to enable it elsewhere, and Kroki always needs an administrator.
## Search

GitLab's project search, through the Projects API `search` parameter and the MCP `list_projects` tool, matches a project's **name, path and description**. It does not read the README; README text is reachable only through code search. So a README earns nothing from keyword work inside GitLab.
## Reading the mode
```bash
glab api "projects/:id?license=true" | jq '{visibility, license: .license.key, description, topics}'

Visibility is `public`, `internal` or `private`. **Internal** means every signed-in user of the instance can see it and nobody else can: use the private-or-internal mode. GitLab projects have no homepage field, and the image a shared link shows is the project avatar; leave it alone for a private or internal project.
## Where GitLab finds the README

The project overview renders a `README`, `index` or `_index` file from the repository root, to anyone who can view the code; people without that permission see the wiki homepage or the issue list instead. Files with a supported markup extension beat plain text, and within each group the first alphabetically wins, so `README.adoc` beats `README.md`, which beats `README.rst`, which beats a plain `README`. A README under `.gitlab/` or `docs/` is not used for the overview.
## Rendering
GitLab renders GitLab Flavored Markdown (GLFM).

- **Table of contents.** GitLab documents no automatic outline for repository files. A `[[_TOC_]]` or `[TOC]` tag on its own line generates one from the headings when the file is rendered, so a long README gets a table of contents without a hand-maintained copy. It is GLFM, so keep it only where the README is read on GitLab.

- **Relative links.** Links to repository files may be relative to the current file, including `../`. They do not cross between the project's wiki and its repository, because the wiki is a separate Git repository.

- **Heading anchors.** Every heading gets one: text lower-cased, everything except letters, numbers, hyphens and underscores removed, spaces turned into hyphens, and a duplicate given an incrementing number starting at 1. Editing a heading changes its anchor and breaks links to it.

- **Alerts.** `> [!note]`, `> [!tip]`, `> [!important]`, `> [!caution]`, `> [!warning]`, introduced in GitLab 17.10, so check a self-managed instance's version before relying on them. Text after the type on the same line replaces the title, as in `> [!warning] Data deletion`, and a `>>> [!note]` multiline blockquote wraps longer content.

- **Diagrams.** A fenced block tagged `mermaid` always renders. On GitLab Self-Managed, a `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` header set to `same-site` or `same-origin` makes Mermaid diagrams fail silently. `plantuml` renders where PlantUML is enabled, as above.
## Maintainer
Resolve the maintainer from the platform, never guess:
```bash
glab api projects/:id | jq '{kind: .namespace.kind, owner: (.owner | if . then {username, name, web_url} else null end)}'

`kind` is `user` for a project in a personal namespace and `group` for a group's project; only a personal project has an `owner`. Write a personal line only for `user`. The profile link is the owner's `web_url`, or MCP `get_user` with the `username`, which returns `name` and `web_url`.
## Stars, following and releases

- **Stars** add a project to the starrer's **Starred** projects list, which is the documented reader benefit: finding it again. Topic pages and the Projects API can sort by number of stars. GitLab documents no recommendation or ranking beyond that sort, so a star line on GitLab claims only that it keeps the project in the reader's list.

- **Following** a user shows their activity in the follower's **Activity** page, on the **Followed users** tab. A user can follow at most 300 people, and either side can turn following off. **There is no documented release notification.**

- **Releases** reach project members who set the project's notification level to **Custom** and select the release event. GitLab documents release emails only for project members, so a non-member has no documented release alert to point at.
